thread.title: Nigeria Inflation Drops to 14.63% in September as Food Inflation Hits 34.40% in Lagos
thread.title_full: Nigeria Inflation Drops to 14.63% in September as Food Inflation Hits 34.40% in Lagos

author: GuardianNigeria
title: Nigeria Inflation Drops to 14.63% in September as Food Inflation Hits 34.40% in Lagos
text:
Nigeria's headline inflation fell to 14.63% in September, the fourth straight monthly decline, but food inflation remains high and Lagos recorded 34.40%.
Nigeria's headline inflation slowed to 14.63 per cent in September, down from 15.39 per cent in August, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS). The decline offers relief for households and businesses after months of rising costs, but food inflation remains high at 19.59 per cent year-on-year, with Lagos recording the highest state-level rate at 34.40 per cent.
Inflation Rate Falls for Fourth Consecutive Month
The September rate is 0.76 percentage points lower than the previous month and 6.35 percentage points below the 20.98 per cent recorded in September 2025. It marks the fourth consecutive monthly decline, following the first drop in June, and is the lowest rate since the NBS changed its CPI methodology in January 2025.
On a month-on-month basis, headline inflation slowed sharply to 0.06 per cent in September from 0.71 per cent in August, indicating that the average price level increased at a much slower pace during the month. The CPI, which measures changes in the prices of goods and services households consume, rose marginally from 146.30 in August to 146.38 in September.
Despite the slowdown, the figures underline the distinction between falling inflation and falling prices. While the rate of price increases has moderated, the report does not indicate that the general price level has returned to previous levels.
Food Inflation Remains High Across States
Food inflation, one of the most consequential components of household expenditure, stood at 19.59 per cent year-on-year in September. That is marginally higher than the 19.57 per cent recorded in August, but lower than the 20.16 per cent in the corresponding month of 2025. More significantly, food inflation declined by 1.55 per cent month-on-month, reversing the 1.02 per cent increase recorded in August.
The NBS attributed the monthly decline to changes in the prices of several food items, including local short-grain rice, maize flour, guinea corn flour, eggs, onions, palm oil, green beans, Irish potatoes, okra, fresh tomatoes, dried green peas and plantain. The decline suggested that food prices eased across a range of important household staples during the month, although the annual inflation rate indicates that food costs remain substantially higher than a year earlier.
Food and non-alcoholic beverages remained the largest driver of headline inflation, contributing 5.85 percentage points, ahead of restaurants and accommodation services (1.89) and transport (1.56). The report also put the average yearly food inflation rate for the 12 months ending September 2026 at 15.72 per cent, compared with 28.37 per cent recorded in September 2025.
A breakdown of inflation across states reveals significant disparities in food price movements, with Lagos recording the highest year-on-year food inflation at 34.40 per cent. Imo State followed with 33.79 per cent, while Ondo recorded 31.49 per cent. At the other end of the scale, Taraba recorded a negative year-on-year food inflation rate of 7.47 per cent, followed by Yobe at negative 0.37 per cent. Borno recorded 2.18 per cent.
The figures highlighted the uneven distribution of food price pressures across the country, with households in some states continuing to face steep increases even as national inflation moderates.
On a month-on-month basis, Imo recorded the highest food inflation at 5.15 per cent, followed by Ondo at 4.46 per cent and Oyo at 3.82 per cent. In contrast, Adamawa recorded a decline of 13.84 per cent, Kano 11.01 per cent and Bauchi 10.21 per cent. The state-level figures suggest that the national decline in food inflation masks substantial differences in local price movements.
Core Inflation Shows Renewed Price Pressures
Core inflation, which excludes volatile agricultural produce and energy prices, stood at 12.95 per cent year-on-year in September, down from 22.11 per cent in September 2025 and 13.29 per cent in August.
However, the month-on-month core inflation rate rose to 1.11 per cent from negative 0.06 per cent in August, indicating renewed price pressures in the underlying basket of goods and services. The average yearly core inflation rate for the 12 months ending September 2026 stood at 16.54 per cent, compared with 25.68 per cent a year earlier.
The contrasting movements in headline and core inflation point to a more complicated price environment than the headline figure alone suggests, as the monthly rise in core inflation indicates that price pressures persist in parts of the economy.
